query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin hafnium (Hf) coating onto a refractory high‐entropy alloy will improve its high‐temperature oxygen resistance by forming a continuous and dense HfO2 protective scale.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., one containing V, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta) in its as-cast or sintered state.
generation.intervention: Deposit a controlled-thickness (≈120 μm) Hf coating onto the alloy surface via a combined processing route (as in the referenced Hf-coated composite process).
generation.conditions: Expose both the Hf-coated and uncoated alloys to an air atmosphere at a high temperature (≈1000 °C) for an extended period (≈50 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of a dense, adherent HfO2 layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The Hf in the coating preferentially oxidizes to form HfO2, which acts as a barrier against oxygen ingress. This protective oxide layer reduces oxidation of the underlying HEA matrix, thereby preserving its structure and mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Hf-coated sample will exhibit a lower weight gain per unit area (indicative of reduced oxide formation) and less surface degradation compared to the uncoated control.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy, which develops a less protective, more porous or spalled oxide scale with higher weight gain when exposed to 1000 °C in air.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvement is expected under high-temperature air exposure around 1000 °C for durations on the order of 50 hours; behavior under significantly higher temperatures or alternate atmospheres remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in oxidation (e.g., percentage weight gain reduction) and long-term adherence of the HfO2 scale under even more extended or varied exposure conditions are not fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set where the refractory high-entropy alloy receives a ≈120 μm Hf coating and another set remains uncoated (control). Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation testing at 1000 °C in air for 50 hours.
measurements: Quantitative weight gain per unit area of each sample before and after exposure
Surface and cross-sectional microstructure examination via SEM/EDS
Phase analysis using XRD to verify formation of a continuous HfO2 layer on the coated sample
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in weight gain and lack evidence of a protective HfO2 scale compared to the uncoated controls, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the continuous exploration of extreme environments such as deep space, deep sea, and outer space, there is an increasing requirement for functional materials capable of withstanding ultra-high and ultra-low temperatures. High-temperature alloys are the main materials serving as core components in frontier technologies such as aerospace and nuclear industries, such as engines, gas turbines, and high-temperature structural parts. These alloys require high strength, high-temperature fatigue resistance, oxidation resistance, and thermal corrosion capability. However, high-temperature and oxidation have become the primary problems that limit the further application of high-temperature alloys in extreme environments. Comprehensive consideration of existing high-temperature oxidation-resistant materials, the main high-temperature oxidation-resistant alloys used in engineering are iron, cobalt, and nickel-based alloys. The cost of iron-based high-temperature alloys is relatively lower, but poorer high-temperature stability. High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application.
